newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian protest vote not seen increasing much.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian protest vote not seen increasing much.

text.p: Official returns on Saturday from Indonesia's general elections indicate there has been no significant increase in the size of a protest vote, political analysts said.
But some said the figure could have been manipulated since any large increase in the figure could be embarrassing for the government of President Suharto.
Election officials said that by Saturday morning, more than 109 million valid votes from Thursday's national polls had been counted, and little changed from previous figures.
They said the ruling Golkar secured 74.26 percent, the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) 22.71 percent and the divided Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) 3.03 percent.
The number of votes counted did not rise significantly overnight, indicating that only a few from remote areas were left, political analysts said.
Indonesia had nearly 125 million eligible voters and the incomplete returns indicate about 90 percent of the electorate voted for one of the three parties, they said.
That implied the size of a protest vote, in which people spoil their ballots or submit blank papers, had not significantly increased from the last election in 1992.

Officials admit nearly half the 10 percent of uncast votes in the 1992 poll were deliberately spoiled. The rest are believed to be normal abstentions, but the government does not release figures other than valid votes.
Independent analyst Arief Budiman said he believed the protest vote, called Golput or "White Group", was much larger.
"We suspect some manipulation by the government but we cannot prove it," he told Reuters. "My sources have told me that in some areas the size of Golput was between 15-20 percent."

The Independent Election Monitoring Committee (KIPP) has said it found evidence of systematic violations of general election rules during its monitoring of Thursday's poll. "There is an indication that there was a systematic violation of the rules due to the fact that the election was organised by the bureaucracy," KIPP chairman Gunawan Mohamad said on Friday.
Gunawan said the size of Golput was "very, very significant" and higher than the three percent obtained by the PDI.
"There are indications that the number of spoiled ballots has increased significantly," he said.
Some economic analysts advised caution until there was some indication on the number of spoiled ballots and abstentions.

"On the surface, things look very good. The government increased its share of the vote substantially," said Desmond Supple, an exotic currencies specialist at BZW Barclays in Singapore. "My concern is if you get a lot of protest votes in the form of spoiled ballots, then any attempt by the government to trumpet the strength or popularity of the success of its policies could create a lot of tensions," he said.
The United States called on Friday for changes in Indonesia's political system, saying that the elections were strictly controlled by the government.
Budiman said he believed the size of Golput was much larger than the returns indicate because of a wave of support for ousted PDI leader Megawati Sukarnoputri.

Megawati, the daughter of late founding president Sukarno and Indonesia's best-known opposition figure, was ousted from the PDI leadership by a government-backed faction last year and barred from standing in the elections.
She said she would not vote as a form of protest, and although she stopped short of an illegal call to boycott the polls, many of her supporters are believed to have done likewise.
Analysts have said the disastrous showing of the PDI is mainly due to her ouster.
